questions.stem: In Young's double-slit experiment, light passing through two narrow slits produces a pattern of bright and dark bands on a screen. What does this pattern show?
options: Light travels in straight lines, because each slit casts a sharp shadow
Light is a longitudinal wave, because the bands are evenly spaced
Light behaves as a wave, because the bands come from interference
Light behaves as a stream of particles that bounce off the slit edges
questions.explanation: Alternating bright and dark bands are an interference pattern: waves from the two slits reinforce in some places and cancel in others. Particles travelling in straight lines would give two bright strips, not many bands. Interference occurs for any wave, so it does not show whether light is transverse or longitudinal.

questions.stem: In a double-slit experiment, what is the condition for a dark band at a point on the screen?
options: The two waves arrive at the point with the same phase and amplitude
The point lies directly opposite one of the slits on the screen
The path difference from the two slits is an odd number of half wavelengths
The path difference from the two slits is a whole number of wavelengths
questions.explanation: When the path difference is ½λ, 1½λ and so on, a crest from one slit arrives with a trough from the other and they cancel: destructive interference. A whole number of wavelengths gives a bright band, where the waves arrive in phase and reinforce.

questions.stem: Light of wavelength 600 nm falls on a pair of slits. What is the path difference from the two slits to the second bright band either side of the central bright band?
questions.explanation: The central band has zero path difference, the first bright band has a path difference of λ and the second has 2λ = 2 × 600 nm = 1.2 × 10⁻⁶ m. The 9.0 × 10⁻⁷ m answer is 1½λ, which gives the second dark band, and 3.0 × 10⁻⁷ m is the first dark band.

questions.stem: Light shows many wave properties. Why can it not be modelled as a mechanical wave?
options: It travels faster than sound, which is the only true mechanical wave
It carries energy, while mechanical waves carry only momentum
It can be reflected, while mechanical waves are always absorbed
It can travel through a vacuum, where there is no medium to vibrate
questions.explanation: Mechanical waves, such as sound or waves on a string, need a medium whose particles oscillate. Light reaches Earth from the Sun across the vacuum of space, so it cannot depend on a medium. Mechanical waves do carry energy and can be reflected, as echoes show.

questions.stem: Which property of light can only be explained if light is a transverse wave?
options: Interference
Diffraction
Reflection
Polarisation
questions.explanation: Polarisation restricts the oscillations to one plane perpendicular to the direction of travel, which is only possible if the oscillations are at right angles to that direction. Interference, diffraction and reflection happen with longitudinal waves such as sound too, so they do not show that light is transverse.

questions.stem: Two polarising filters are placed one behind the other, and the second is rotated until no light gets through. Why can the same thing never be done with sound waves?
options: Sound has too long a wavelength to pass through a polarising filter
Sound is a mechanical wave, so it cannot be absorbed by a filter
Sound travels too slowly for the filters to select a single plane
Sound is longitudinal, so it has no transverse oscillation to filter
questions.explanation: A polarising filter passes only the transverse oscillations in one plane, and crossed filters block both planes. Sound oscillates along its direction of travel, so there is no plane of oscillation to select. Sound can be absorbed by materials, so that is not the reason.

questions.stem: Electrons in a radio transmitter's antenna oscillate at 100 MHz. What is the wavelength of the electromagnetic waves produced?
questions.explanation: Oscillating charges produce EM waves of the same frequency, 100 MHz. Then λ = c/f = 3.00 × 10⁸/(1.00 × 10⁸) = 3.0 m. The 0.33 m answer inverts the ratio to f/c, and 30 m comes from using 10 MHz.

questions.stem: What is a black body?
options: An ideal object that emits no radiation at any temperature because it absorbs all light falling on it
Any object that appears black in visible light because it reflects only infrared radiation
An object hot enough to emit all colours of visible light equally, so that it appears white
An ideal object that absorbs all radiation falling on it and emits a spectrum set only by its temperature
questions.explanation: A black body absorbs every wavelength that falls on it, and its emitted thermal radiation depends only on its temperature, not its material. It does emit radiation; a hot black body such as a star can be very bright. Stars and furnace openings are close to black bodies.

questions.stem: Before quantum theory, the classical wave model predicted the spectrum of a black body. What did it predict that disagreed with observations?
options: The intensity would keep increasing at shorter wavelengths without limit
The intensity would be zero at all wavelengths shorter than visible light
The intensity would be the same at all wavelengths for every temperature
The intensity would peak at a wavelength that did not depend on temperature
questions.explanation: The classical model predicted ever-increasing emission towards short wavelengths, the ultraviolet catastrophe, implying infinite total energy. Observed spectra rise to a peak and then fall at short wavelengths. A particle model, with energy emitted in quanta E = hf, explained the true shape.

questions.stem: How did treating radiation as emitted in quanta of energy E = hf explain the fall in black body intensity at short wavelengths?
options: Short-wavelength quanta have high energy, so few are emitted at a given temperature
Short-wavelength quanta have low energy, so they cannot escape the black body
Short-wavelength quanta travel more slowly, so fewer reach the detector each second
Short-wavelength quanta are absorbed by the air before they can be measured
questions.explanation: A quantum of high frequency, short-wavelength radiation needs a lot of energy, E = hf, and at a given temperature few oscillators have enough to emit one. So emission falls away at short wavelengths instead of growing without limit. All EM radiation travels at c in a vacuum.

questions.stem: A black body is heated from 3000 K to 6000 K. How does its emission spectrum change?
options: The peak moves to longer wavelengths and the intensity rises at all wavelengths
The peak stays at the same wavelength but becomes much more intense
The peak moves to shorter wavelengths but the total intensity stays the same
The peak moves to shorter wavelengths and the intensity rises at all wavelengths
questions.explanation: A hotter black body emits more at every wavelength, and its peak shifts to shorter wavelengths. This is why heated metal glows red, then orange, then white. The total power emitted increases strongly with temperature, so it cannot stay the same.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon of green light of wavelength 500 nm?
questions.explanation: E = hc/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸/(500 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, which is about 2.5 eV. The 1.3 × 10⁻²⁷ value is h/λ, the photon's momentum in kg m s⁻¹, and 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ J confuses the energy in electronvolts with joules.

questions.stem: What is the momentum of a photon of energy 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J?
options: 4.4 × 10⁻³⁶ kg m s⁻¹
1.3 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m s⁻¹
1.2 × 10⁻¹⁰ kg m s⁻¹
0 kg m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: For a photon E = pc, so p = E/c = 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹/(3.00 × 10⁸) ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m s⁻¹. A photon has no mass but it does carry momentum, which is why light exerts a small pressure. Multiplying by c gives 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁰, and dividing by c² gives 4.4 × 10⁻³⁶.

questions.stem: What is the frequency of a photon with an energy of 3.0 eV?
options: 4.5 × 10³³ Hz
1.4 × 10¹⁴ Hz
2.4 × 10¹⁵ Hz
7.2 × 10¹⁴ Hz
questions.explanation: Convert to joules first: 3.0 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Then f = E/h = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹/(6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) ≈ 7.2 × 10¹⁴ Hz, in the violet. Dividing 3.0 by h without converting gives 4.5 × 10³³ Hz.

questions.stem: A 5.0 mW laser pointer emits red light of wavelength 650 nm. About how many photons does it emit each second?
questions.explanation: Each photon has E = hc/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸/(650 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ 3.06 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. The number per second is the power divided by the photon energy: 5.0 × 10⁻³/(3.06 × 10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 1.6 × 10¹⁶. Using 5.0 W instead of 5.0 mW gives 1.6 × 10¹⁹, and 3.1 × 10⁻¹⁹ is the energy of one photon.

questions.stem: What is the photoelectric effect?
options: The emission of electrons from a metal surface when light of high enough frequency falls on it
The emission of light from a metal surface when a current of electrons passes through it
The bending of light around the edges of a metal surface that is struck by electrons
The heating of a metal surface by light until electrons boil off its surface
questions.explanation: In the photoelectric effect, light shining on a metal ejects electrons, called photoelectrons, but only if its frequency is above a threshold for that metal. Emission is immediate, so it is not a heating effect. Light emitted when electrons strike a material is a different process.

questions.stem: Light above the threshold frequency shines on a metal. The intensity is doubled while the frequency is kept the same. What happens to the photoelectrons?
options: The same number are emitted, with twice the maximum kinetic energy
Twice as many are emitted, each with twice the maximum kinetic energy
The same number are emitted, with the same maximum kinetic energy
Twice as many are emitted, with the same maximum kinetic energy
questions.explanation: Doubling the intensity at the same frequency doubles the number of photons arriving each second, each with the same energy hf. Each photon ejects at most one electron, so twice as many are emitted, but the maximum kinetic energy, hf − φ, is unchanged.

questions.stem: Very bright red light shines on a metal and no electrons are emitted, but dim violet light ejects electrons at once. How does the photon model explain this?
options: Violet light is more intense than red light, so it delivers more energy
Each red photon has less energy than the work function, however many arrive
Red light waves are too long to fit into the spaces between the metal atoms
Red light takes longer to build up enough energy in each electron to free it
questions.explanation: An electron absorbs one photon at a time, so it escapes only if a single photon's energy, hf, exceeds the work function. Red photons have too little energy, and more of them cannot add up for one electron. The wave model wrongly predicted that bright light of any frequency would eventually free electrons.

questions.stem: Which observation of the photoelectric effect could the wave model of light not explain?
options: Electrons are emitted from metals but not from good insulators
Electrons leave the surface with a range of kinetic energies
Electrons are emitted immediately, even when the light is very dim
The number of electrons emitted increases with the light's intensity
questions.explanation: In the wave model, energy spreads evenly over the wave front, so dim light should take time to give an electron enough energy to escape. In fact emission is instantaneous above the threshold frequency, because each photon delivers its energy in one go. More electrons with brighter light fits both models.

questions.stem: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 200 nm shines on a metal with a work function of 4.3 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons?
options: 6.2 eV
4.3 eV
1.9 eV
questions.explanation: The photon energy is hc/λ = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸/(200 × 10⁻⁹) ≈ 9.9 × 10⁻¹⁹ J ≈ 6.2 eV. Then Ek = hf − φ = 6.2 − 4.3 ≈ 1.9 eV. The 6.2 eV answer forgets to subtract the work function, and 10.5 eV adds it instead.

questions.stem: A metal has a work function of 2.3 eV. What is its threshold frequency?
options: 3.5 × 10³³ Hz
1.7 × 10¹⁴ Hz
5.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz
questions.explanation: At the threshold frequency a photon's energy just equals the work function, so f₀ = φ/h = 2.3 × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹/(6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) ≈ 5.6 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Leaving φ in electronvolts gives 3.5 × 10³³ Hz, and h/φ gives 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁵.

questions.stem: A student plots the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against the frequency of the light for one metal. What does the gradient of the straight line give?
options: The speed of light
Planck's constant
The work function
The threshold frequency
questions.explanation: Ek = hf − φ has the form y = mx + c, so the gradient is h for every metal. The intercept on the frequency axis is the threshold frequency, and the intercept on the energy axis is −φ. This is how Planck's constant can be found from the photoelectric effect.

questions.stem: For one metal, photoelectrons have a maximum kinetic energy of 0.40 eV with light of 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz and 1.23 eV with light of 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz. What value of Planck's constant do these results give?
questions.explanation: The gradient is (1.23 − 0.40)/(8.0 × 10¹⁴ − 6.0 × 10¹⁴) = 4.15 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s. Converting to joules: 4.15 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. The 4.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ value is the gradient left in eV s but labelled J s.

questions.stem: Using the same results (0.40 eV at 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz and a gradient of 4.15 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s), what is the work function of the metal?
options: 1.6 eV
2.1 eV
2.5 eV
questions.explanation: From Ek = hf − φ, φ = hf − Ek = 4.15 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 6.0 × 10¹⁴ − 0.40 = 2.49 − 0.40 ≈ 2.1 eV. The 2.5 eV answer is the photon energy, forgetting to subtract the kinetic energy, and 0.40 eV is the kinetic energy itself.

questions.stem: Why can the light from a distant star be used to identify the elements in its outer layers?
options: Each element changes the speed of the light that passes through it
Each element absorbs every wavelength except its characteristic colour
Each element emits and absorbs its own unique set of wavelengths
Each element produces a continuous spectrum of a different brightness
questions.explanation: Every element has its own energy levels, so it emits and absorbs a unique pattern of wavelengths, like a fingerprint. Dark absorption lines in starlight match the emission lines of elements measured in the laboratory. This is the basis of spectral analysis.

questions.stem: White light passes through cool hydrogen gas and then through a spectroscope. What is observed?
options: A continuous spectrum crossed by dark lines at hydrogen's emission wavelengths
Bright coloured lines on a dark background at hydrogen's emission wavelengths
A continuous spectrum with no lines, since hydrogen is transparent
A continuous spectrum crossed by dark lines at wavelengths hydrogen cannot emit
questions.explanation: Hydrogen atoms absorb photons whose energies match the differences between their energy levels, removing those wavelengths and leaving dark lines. These are the same wavelengths hydrogen emits when hot, because the same level differences are involved. Bright lines on a dark background would be an emission spectrum.

questions.stem: In the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom, when does the atom emit a photon?
options: When its electron rises from a lower energy level to a higher one
When its electron stays in any orbit above the ground state
When its electron drops from a higher energy level to a lower one
When its electron moves faster around a fixed orbit
questions.explanation: Bohr proposed that electrons occupy fixed energy levels without radiating, and that a photon of energy E₂ − E₁ = hf is emitted when the electron drops between levels. Rising to a higher level requires energy to be absorbed, not emitted.

questions.stem: The hydrogen energy levels are E₁ = −13.6 eV, E₂ = −3.40 eV and E₃ = −1.51 eV. What is the wavelength of the photon emitted when an electron drops from n = 3 to n = 2?
questions.explanation: The photon energy is −1.51 − (−3.40) = 1.89 eV = 3.02 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, so λ = hc/E ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻⁷ m, the red line of hydrogen. Using only the 3.40 eV of level 2 gives 3.7 × 10⁻⁷ m, and the drop from n = 3 to n = 1 gives 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ m, in the ultraviolet.

questions.stem: Hydrogen atoms in the ground state (−13.6 eV) are exposed to photons. The levels above it are −3.40 eV, −1.51 eV and −0.85 eV. Which photon energy can be absorbed?
questions.explanation: A photon is absorbed only if its energy exactly matches a gap from the ground state: 10.2 eV (to n = 2), 12.1 eV (to n = 3) or 12.8 eV (to n = 4). An 11.0 eV photon matches no gap, so it passes through. The 3.40 eV and 1.51 eV values are level energies, not gaps from the ground state.

questions.stem: A hydrogen atom in its ground state (−13.6 eV) is struck by an electron with 11.0 eV of kinetic energy. The first excited state is −3.40 eV. What can happen?
options: Nothing, because 11.0 eV does not match an energy gap
The atom is ionised and the electron keeps 2.6 eV
The atom is raised to n = 2 and emits a 0.8 eV photon
The atom is raised to n = 2 and the electron keeps 0.8 eV
questions.explanation: Unlike a photon, which must be absorbed whole, a colliding electron can give up just part of its energy. It can supply the 10.2 eV needed to reach n = 2 and keep the remaining 0.8 eV. Ionisation needs 13.6 eV, more than the electron has.

questions.stem: What is the ionisation energy of a hydrogen atom in its ground state, where the electron's energy is −13.6 eV?
options: 0 eV
questions.explanation: Ionisation means raising the electron to E = 0, where it is free of the atom, so 0 − (−13.6) = 13.6 eV is needed. The 10.2 eV only reaches the first excited state, which is still bound.

questions.stem: A fluorescent mineral glows green under ultraviolet light. How does the Bohr model explain why it emits a longer wavelength than it absorbs?
options: The electron returns to the ground state in smaller steps, each emitting a lower-energy photon
The electron absorbs several ultraviolet photons and releases their energy as one green photon
The ultraviolet photon slows down inside the mineral, which lengthens its wavelength
The electron rises in several small steps, emitting green light at each step upward
questions.explanation: Absorbing an ultraviolet photon lifts an electron to a high level. It then falls back through intermediate levels, and each smaller drop emits a photon of lower energy and so longer wavelength, such as green light. Light does slow in a material, but its frequency, and so its energy, does not change.

questions.stem: What distinguishes phosphorescence from fluorescence?
options: Phosphorescent materials emit shorter wavelengths than the light they absorb
Phosphorescent materials glow only while ultraviolet light is shining on them
Phosphorescent materials emit light by heating, not by electron transitions
Phosphorescent materials keep glowing after the exciting light is removed
questions.explanation: In phosphorescence electrons are held in metastable states for a long time before dropping, so the glow continues after the source is removed, as in glow-in-the-dark paint. Fluorescence stops almost at once when the source is switched off. Both involve electron transitions and emit longer wavelengths than they absorb.

questions.stem: In a fluorescent tube, an electric discharge excites mercury vapour, which emits mainly ultraviolet light. What is the role of the coating on the inside of the glass?
options: It reflects the ultraviolet back into the tube to excite more mercury
It conducts the current so the mercury vapour can be excited
It converts visible light from the mercury into ultraviolet light
It absorbs the ultraviolet and fluoresces, emitting visible light
questions.explanation: The phosphor coating absorbs ultraviolet photons and re-emits lower-energy visible photons by fluorescence, so the tube gives useful light. Converting visible light into ultraviolet would need photons to gain energy, which fluorescence cannot do.

questions.stem: In an X-ray tube, fast electrons strike a metal target. How does the Bohr model explain the sharp lines in the X-ray spectrum?
options: The fast electrons are slowed gradually, emitting X-rays of every wavelength
The target atoms are heated until they glow at X-ray wavelengths
The fast electrons are absorbed by the target nuclei, which emit X-rays
An electron knocked out of an inner shell is replaced by one falling from a higher level
questions.explanation: A fast electron can eject an electron from an inner energy level of a target atom. An electron from a higher level drops into the vacancy and emits an X-ray photon whose energy equals the gap, which is characteristic of the target metal. The slowing of electrons gives the continuous background, not the sharp lines.

questions.stem: An X-ray tube accelerates electrons through 30 kV. What is the shortest wavelength of X-ray it can produce?
questions.explanation: Each electron gains qV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 30 × 10³ = 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁵ J. The shortest wavelength is from an electron giving all of this to one photon: λ = hc/E = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸/(4.8 × 10⁻¹⁵) ≈ 4.1 × 10⁻¹¹ m. Using 30 V instead of 30 kV gives 4.1 × 10⁻⁸ m.

questions.stem: An electron in a diffraction experiment moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. What is its de Broglie wavelength?
questions.explanation: λ = h/p = h/(mv) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × 2.0 × 10⁶) ≈ 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, similar to the spacing of atoms in a crystal. Using the proton mass gives 2.0 × 10⁻¹³ m, and 1.8 × 10⁻²⁴ is the electron's momentum, not its wavelength.

questions.stem: Which observation provides direct evidence that electrons have wave properties?
options: Electrons are ejected from a metal surface when ultraviolet light shines on it
Electrons are deflected into a circular path when moving through a magnetic field
Electrons emit photons of definite energies when they drop between energy levels
A beam of electrons produces a diffraction pattern when passed through a crystal
questions.explanation: Diffraction and interference are wave behaviours, and electron beams produce diffraction patterns when they pass through crystals, whose atomic spacing is close to the electrons' de Broglie wavelength. The photoelectric effect shows the particle nature of light, not the wave nature of electrons.

questions.stem: In a double-slit experiment, electrons are fired one at a time. Each arrives as a single dot on the screen, but after many arrive the dots form bright and dark bands. What does this show?
options: The electrons interfere with each other, so the pattern needs many at once
The electrons are particles that bounce off the slit edges into the bands
The screen produces the bands, since single electrons cannot interfere
Each electron behaves as a wave passing through both slits and arrives as a particle
questions.explanation: Because the electrons pass through one at a time, the bands cannot come from electrons interfering with each other. Each electron's wave goes through both slits and interferes, setting where it is likely to land, but it is detected as a single particle. The same result occurs with single photons, showing wave-particle duality.

questions.stem: A cricket ball of mass 0.16 kg moves at 40 m s⁻¹. Why is its wave nature never observed?
options: Its de Broglie wavelength, about 10⁻³⁴ m, is far smaller than any gap it could pass
Its de Broglie wavelength, about 10³⁴ m, is far larger than any gap it could pass
Only charged particles such as electrons have a de Broglie wavelength
Only objects travelling close to the speed of light show wave properties
questions.explanation: λ = h/(mv) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(0.16 × 40) ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻³⁴ m, far smaller than an atomic nucleus, so no diffraction can be seen. All moving matter has a de Broglie wavelength, charged or not, at any speed.
